stories.headline: Kestrel's free model catches the big labs at coding
stories.dek: The open-weight Kestrel 2 lands within two points of the best closed models on coding benchmarks, and anyone can download it today.
stories.body:
Kestrel AI released Kestrel 2 on Monday, an open-weight language model that scores 71.4 percent on the CodeArena benchmark, two points behind the best closed model the benchmark's maintainers have tested. The previous best open model scored 58 percent.

The weights are published under a license that allows commercial use, with one restriction: companies with more than 700 million monthly users need a separate agreement. The full model has 405 billion parameters, but Kestrel also released a 70-billion-parameter version that The Byte Ledger reports runs at usable speed on a workstation with two high-end consumer GPUs.

Kestrel says the jump comes mostly from training data rather than size. The company generated roughly 40 billion tokens of synthetic programming exercises, then filtered them by running the code and keeping only solutions that passed their tests. It describes the method in a 60-page technical report but has not released the dataset itself.

Independent testing is still thin. Kernel Post ran the 70B version on 100 real bug-fix tasks from open-source projects and found it solved 48, compared with 61 for a leading closed model, so the benchmark gap may understate the difference on messy, real-world code. Long-context performance also drops off past 64,000 tokens, according to the same test.

On Hacker News, where the release drew more than 1,200 comments, developers focused on the license and on whether the synthetic-data method can be reproduced. Several noted that the report leaves out how many GPU hours training took, which makes the cost hard to compare.

Kestrel says a version tuned for agents, with tool calling built in, will follow "within weeks".
key_points: Scores 71.4% on CodeArena, two points behind the best closed model
Free for commercial use, except for the very largest companies
A 70B version runs on a workstation with two consumer GPUs
Early real-world tests show a wider gap than the benchmark
stories.why_it_matters: If the results hold up, teams can run near-frontier coding help on their own hardware, which changes the cost and privacy math for AI coding tools.

stories.headline: Popular npm package hijacked to steal cloud keys
stories.dek: A poisoned release of tinyfetchr, downloaded nine million times a week, quietly sent environment variables to an attacker for six hours.
stories.body:
Attackers published a malicious version of tinyfetchr, a small HTTP helper used by thousands of JavaScript projects, after taking over a maintainer's account on Sunday night. Version 4.2.1 contained an install script that collected environment variables, including cloud access keys and CI tokens, and sent them to a remote server.

The release was live for about six hours before the registry pulled it. Kernel Post estimates it was installed around 180,000 times in that window, most of them by automated CI pipelines that pick up new patch versions without review.

The maintainer says the account had two-factor authentication, but a session token was stolen through a phishing page that imitated the registry's login. Circuit Weekly reports that the same server received data from two smaller packages hijacked in October.

Anyone who installed 4.2.1 should rotate every secret the build machine could see. Lockfiles that pin an earlier version were not affected.
key_points: Version 4.2.1 stole environment variables during install
Live for six hours; about 180,000 installs, mostly CI
Rotate secrets if your builds pulled 4.2.1; pinned lockfiles were safe
stories.why_it_matters: It is another reminder that unpinned dependencies in CI give every maintainer's account the keys to your cloud.

stories.headline: Arcwave's new desktop chip is faster, cooler and cheaper
stories.dek: First reviews of the Arcwave R9 show 18 percent more multi-core speed than last year's flagship, at a lower launch price.
stories.body:
Reviews of Arcwave's R9 desktop processor went live on Tuesday, and the picture is unusually consistent: about 18 percent faster in multi-threaded work than last year's top chip, roughly the same in games, and noticeably cooler under load.

Circuit Weekly measured a peak of 168 watts in a long rendering test, down from 230 on the previous generation, which means a mid-range air cooler is enough. The Byte Ledger found the chip ran its full test suite without throttling in a small-form-factor case.

The R9 launches at €549, €50 less than its predecessor did. It needs a new motherboard socket, though, and early boards start at around €220.

For gaming alone, both outlets say last year's chip is still the better deal while it is discounted.
key_points: About 18% faster multi-core, similar gaming performance
Peak power down from 230 W to 168 W
€549 at launch, but needs a new motherboard
stories.why_it_matters: Lower power draw means quieter, smaller workstations without giving up speed.

stories.headline: Model makers sign up to a shared safety test suite
stories.dek: Eleven AI labs will run the same 300 safety tests before each major release and publish the scores.
stories.body:
The Open Model Standards Group, an industry body formed last year, published its first common safety test suite on Monday. Eleven labs have agreed to run its 300 tests, covering areas such as cyberattack assistance and dangerous chemistry, before every major model release, and to publish the results within two weeks.

Critics point out that the labs wrote the tests themselves and that publishing scores is voluntary in practice, since there is no penalty for skipping it.
key_points: 300 shared tests before every major release
Eleven labs signed up
No penalty for skipping

stories.headline: Coding agents now write a third of new code at mid-size firms
stories.dek: A survey of 2,000 developers finds agent-written code is common, but most teams still review every line.
stories.body:
Kernel Post's annual developer survey found that at companies with 100 to 1,000 engineers, AI agents now produce about 34 percent of newly merged code, up from 12 percent a year ago. Ninety percent of respondents said every agent change still goes through human review.

The biggest complaint was not quality but review fatigue: half said agents produce more changes than their team can comfortably read.
key_points: 34% of new code at mid-size firms, up from 12%
90% review every agent change
Review fatigue is the top complaint

stories.headline: Ferrous terminal hits 1.0 after four years
stories.dek: The GPU-accelerated terminal written in Rust adds split panes, a plugin API and a stable config format.
stories.body:
Ferrous, an open-source terminal emulator, reached version 1.0 on Monday. The release freezes the configuration format, adds split panes and tabs, and ships a plugin API that lets extensions add status bars and custom key bindings.

The project's benchmarks show it rendering large log files about three times faster than the default terminals on macOS and Linux. Windows support remains experimental.
key_points: Stable config format and plugin API
Split panes and tabs
Windows support still experimental

stories.headline: Three browsers agree on a common way to move passkeys
stories.dek: A shared export format means passkeys will no longer be stuck in the password manager that created them.
stories.body:
Three major browser makers said on Monday they will support a common format for exporting and importing passkeys, starting with releases due in the first quarter. Until now, moving passkeys between password managers has mostly meant creating new ones site by site.

The format encrypts the export with a one-time key shown on screen, so a stolen export file is useless on its own.
key_points: Common passkey export format
Ships early next year
Exports are encrypted with a one-time key

stories.headline: SSD prices fall for a third straight month

stories.body:
Average prices for consumer SSDs fell another 6 percent in October, according to price-tracking data compiled by The Byte Ledger. A typical 2 TB drive now sells for about €95.

Analysts expect prices to bottom out in December as manufacturers cut production.
key_points: Down 6% in October
2 TB for about €95
Expected to bottom out in December

opinion.headline: Build the PC this winter, not next year
opinion.dek: Cheaper chips, falling SSD prices and discounted graphics cards line up for once, and waiting for next year's parts is the worse bet.
opinion.body:
A 2 TB SSD costs about €95 this month, the lowest price in almost two years, according to The Byte Ledger. That alone would not be a reason to build a computer. It is the company it keeps that matters.

For the first time in a while, every big part of a desktop is getting cheaper or better at the same moment. Anyone who has been putting off an upgrade should stop waiting.

Start with the processor. Circuit Weekly and The Byte Ledger found Arcwave's new R9 about 18 percent faster than last year's flagship in multi-threaded work, and it launched at a lower price. It also runs cool enough for a mid-range air cooler, which is money saved twice.

Graphics cards point the same way. Entry-level cards sell for about 10 percent under their launch prices, Circuit Weekly reports, as stores clear stock ahead of next year's refresh.

The case for waiting is real: new parts always come, and analysts quoted by The Byte Ledger expect SSD prices to bottom out in December. But a bottom is only visible afterward, and the saving left on a €95 drive is small.

Cheap parts now are worth more than better parts later.

So buy the processor and the storage this winter, and pick the graphics card last, when the refresh makes the old models cheaper still.
opinion.pull_quote: Cheap parts now are worth more than better parts later.
opinion.thesis: With CPU, SSD and GPU prices all falling at once, building a PC now beats waiting for next year's parts.
